title: Step-by-Step: Rent Board License and Notice
description: The direct answer to the licensing question, the 12-step official process, and how it applies to the two anonymized units.

sections.title: Your question first: does an individual owner need a Rent Board license?

rows.label: Must an individual property owner (not a corporation) get a Rent Increase License before raising rent?
rows.value: Yes. A landlord must have a current Rent Increase License on file before any annual or banked increase can take effect. The requirement is tied to the unit being under San Francisco rent control, not to the owner's size or corporate status.
rows.notes: No owner-type, individual-owner or small-portfolio exemption appears on the official pages.

rows.label: Must the owner report into the Rent Board Housing Inventory first?
rows.value: Yes. SF.gov states that all owners of residential property are required to report into the Housing Inventory; a rent increase license is generated for units reported as tenant-occupied.
rows.notes: Reporting is free; the annual deadline is March 1.

rows.label: Is there a small-owner or fewer-than-10-unit exemption?
rows.value: No exemption found. Owners of condominiums and buildings with fewer than 10 residential units have been required to report since March 1, 2023, with updates due every March 1.
rows.notes: Relevant to this two-unit building if the units are rent-controlled.

rows.label: Does "informing the Rent Board" mean filing each increase notice?
rows.value: The official pages describe the license as arising from the annual Housing Inventory report. No separate filing of an individual increase notice with the Rent Board is described, and the license does not need to be included with the notice.
rows.notes: Read as the absence of a stated requirement; confirm with a Rent Board counselor.

rows.label: What happens if a notice goes into effect without a current license?
rows.value: SF.gov says a rent increase notice that goes into effect while the unit is unlicensed may be null and void (possibly for multiple years); the tenant may be entitled to a rent refund and may file a Tenant Petition for Unlawful Rent Increase for a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge.
rows.notes: Tenants can check license status in the portal for the effective date of the increase.

rows.label: Does the license requirement cover every kind of increase?
rows.value: SF.gov ties the license to annual allowable and banked increases on rent-controlled units, and states it is not required for Section 6.14/Costa-Hawkins increases or for passthroughs allowed under the Rent Ordinance.
rows.notes: Those other increases have their own notice and petition rules.

rows.label: Is the Housing Inventory information public?
rows.value: Yes. SF.gov states that the information entered in the Housing Inventory submission is public, and may include name and business, contact information, approximate square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms and vacancy/occupancy history.
rows.notes: Privacy note: the filing itself publishes the owner's name and business contact information.

rows.label: What does the Rent Ordinance itself say?
rows.value: Section 37.3(a)(1): "A landlord who has reported the required information about their rental unit to the Rent Board as set forth in Section 37.15 shall have a license to impose annually a rent increase which does not exceed a tenant's base rent by more than 60% of said published increase." Form 571 adds that the annual increase may be imposed "without filing a petition at the Rent Board."
rows.notes: The license precondition is written into the ordinance, not just the SF.gov summaries.

rows.label: Does the license requirement apply if the unit is not rent-controlled?
rows.value: No. SF.gov states that the Rent Increase License rules apply only to units under San Francisco rent control.
rows.notes: Coverage of the specific address is still unverified in this case.

rows.label: Step 1 - Confirm the unit is under the Rent Ordinance
rows.value: Check the building on the SF Planning Property Information Map: many units built on or before June 13, 1979 that are not single-family dwellings have rent control; partial exemptions exist.
rows.notes: Exact address not supplied in this case.

rows.label: Step 2 - Create a Rent Board Portal account
rows.value: Owners create an account in the Rent Board Portal to reach the Housing Inventory and the license record.
rows.notes: Paper filings can be emailed or dropped off at the Rent Board office.

rows.label: Step 3 - Report each unit into the Housing Inventory
rows.value: Report by March 1 each year (buildings under 10 units since March 1, 2023) under penalty of perjury: owner or manager contact, square footage, bedrooms, bathrooms, occupancy date and base rent in $250 increments.
rows.notes: Reporting is free; no monetary penalty is assessed for late filing.

rows.label: Step 4 - Confirm a current Rent Increase License
rows.value: The license is generated for tenant-occupied units after reporting. It must be on file and current on the effective date of the increase, not merely later.
rows.notes: Check status by address or APN in the portal.

rows.label: Step 5 - Fix the anniversary date
rows.value: The first annual increase may be imposed 12 months after the lease began; after an increase, the increase date becomes the anniversary date and the next increase needs at least 12 more months.
rows.notes: A later increase date becomes the new anniversary date.

rows.label: Step 6 - Use the rate in effect on the effective date
rows.value: 1.6% for increases effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027. Use the percentage in effect on the increase date, not the notice date.
rows.notes: The rate for increases on or after 3/1/27 is not yet published.

rows.label: Step 7 - Decide whether a banked increase applies
rows.value: A skipped increase is only banked if at least 24 full months pass without any rent increase; banked percentages are added together, never compounded or prorated, and never carry to a new tenant.
rows.notes: SF.gov examples describe elapsed time differently - flagged as F03.

rows.label: Step 8 - Calculate on base rent only and do not round up
rows.value: Multiply base rent (including parking or storage charges) by the total percentage; temporary passthroughs and fluctuating charges are excluded, and the result is not rounded up to the nearest dollar.
rows.notes: See the Calculations page for the illustrative arithmetic.

rows.label: Step 9 - File any petition or worksheet before the notice
rows.value: Capital improvement, operating and maintenance, utility, comparable-rent and bond/water passthrough increases each have their own petition or worksheet rules that apply before the increase is noticed.
rows.notes: Not needed for a plain annual or banked increase.

rows.label: Step 10 - Serve written notice with the required contents
rows.value: At least 30 days' written notice, or 90 days if the increase by itself or combined with another increase in the same year is more than 10%; add 5 days if mailed. State the dollar amount, the percentage, the effective date and any banked portion.
rows.notes: Civil Code 827 requires longer notice in some cases.

rows.label: Step 11 - Deliver it properly and keep proof
rows.value: Personal delivery or mail under Civil Code 827 and Code of Civil Procedure 1013; keep the notice, proof of service and the license record with the unit file.
rows.notes: The license need not be attached to the notice.

rows.label: Step 12 - Expect tenant-side review and apply the same rule to each unit
rows.value: Tenant petitions are free and have no filing deadline for an unlawful increase; a tenant may search the portal for license status. Apply the same written, neutral, dated process to every eligible unit.
rows.notes: No rule requires raising both units - see Analysis.

sections.title: How this applies to the two anonymized units

rows.label: Unit 1 - earliest annual increase under the stated lease date
rows.value: With a February 1, 2025 lease start, the first annual increase could have been given on February 1, 2026; any later increase date uses the rate in effect on that date.
rows.notes: Derived from the official timing rule plus the owner-supplied date; no increase history was supplied.

rows.label: Unit 1 - effect of the April 1, 2026 continuing tenancy at $3,995
rows.value: Adding an occupant and keeping the same rent does not by itself create a new tenancy or a market-rate reset, and extra rent for an additional occupant is unlawful.
rows.notes: Whether the April 1, 2026 document restarted the lease or anniversary date is unverified - see Anonymized Case.

rows.label: Unit 2 - earliest annual increase under the stated lease date
rows.value: With a June 1, 2019 lease start, annual increases were available from June 1, 2020; an increase effective now uses the 1.6% rate plus any properly banked increases.
rows.notes: Prior increases since 2019 were not supplied, so no banked amount is computed.

rows.label: Banked totals can push one notice above 10%
rows.value: If a correctly banked total plus the current annual rate exceeds 10%, the notice must be 90 days rather than 30 days.
rows.notes: No banked percentage is asserted for either unit.

rows.label: An increase effective on or after March 1, 2027
rows.notes: The next allowable rate has not been published; blank rather than estimated.

rows.label: License status for either unit
rows.notes: Owner has not stated whether each unit is reported and licensed; check the portal.
